item.title: [Translation] Friends Don’t Let Friends Use Ollama
item.description:
Below is a translation of the article "Friends Don’t Let Friends Use Ollama", published on Sleeping Robots in April 2026. Since Ollama has changed significantly in the intervening months, I have added several comments to the translation and a note at the end of the article, where I have updated key technical details as of September 2026. Ollama became popular because it was the first to offer a simple interface on top of llama.cpp. And then for years it tried not to remind people what it actually worked on, misled users, and finally turned towards the cloud – all on venture money raised around someone else's engine. Here is the full story – and why alternatives look better today. Ollama is the most popular way to run large language models locally. And perhaps it shouldn't be. Its position is primarily due to the fact that it was first: the first tool that made llama.cpp accessible to people who didn't want to compile C++ or write server configurations themselves. At the time, this was indeed a useful contribution. But then the project systematically obscured the origin of the technology it worked on for years, misled users about what exactly they were running, and moved further and further away from the "local first" principle that initially earned it trust. And all this – in parallel with attracting venture capital investments. This is not an attempt to find "truth somewhere in the middle." I used Ollama. Then I stopped. Below is why, in my opinion, you should do the same. Read about Ollama and its history

item.title: AI Forgot About Energy? The Paradox of AI Market Research in Russia
item.description:
I saw figures from an AIANA study – new analytics on the Russian AI market. The volume is estimated at 316.1 billion rubles (as of the end of 2025). The main customer, logically, is business: 71.9% of revenue comes from B2B. 98.4 billion rubles are for AI hardware and physical infrastructure. This is 31.1% of the market – the largest segment by revenue. For me, this is the main point: digital confirmation that the AI market is supported not only by models, applications, and prompts, but by "hardware." But then things get interesting. The largest segment of hardware is computing "hardware." The first question that arose for me as someone from the energy sector was: was electricity forgotten in this segment? As it turned out a couple of scrolls down, it wasn't forgotten. It's just that in business logic, energy is currently consciously left outside the AI market. Let's figure out why and what the risks are. How accurately does the picture without energy convey the real possibilities of launching new AI projects? Read more

item.title: A Method for Visualizing N-Dimensional Embeddings in Three-Dimensional Space
item.description:
A method for visualizing n-dimensional embeddings in three-dimensional space. Typically, when discussing embedding visualization (or, as we now know, n-dimensional vectors), it refers to mapping a set of these vectors into a two- or three-dimensional space with dimensionality reduction. However, for human analysis of vectors, it can also be useful to visualize an individual vector. In this case, it's possible to compare the 'shape' of objects representing vectors and infer the proximity of compared vectors based on the similarity of these shapes. It would also be interesting to visualize a vector during neural network training iterations and observe changes in the vector's 'shape' as the model trains. This approach avoids the data loss drawback of commonly used dimensionality reduction methods for vector mapping. Read more

item.title: Let's try again, Misha: speculative decoding from draft to verification
item.description:
A small model quickly drafts a few next tokens, and a large one verifies the whole batch in one pass. Matching tokens are kept, and at the first divergence, the large model rewrites the continuation itself, so the acceleration doesn't change the response distribution. In speculative decoding, the large model literally tells the draft model: "Let's try again, Misha." At first glance, it seems that acceleration here is necessarily bought at the cost of quality. But no: this is precisely the case where generation can be accelerated without such a compromise. Next, we will analyze the entire cycle: how the draft model works, by what rule tokens are accepted, what the size of the draft should be, why the same tokenizer is important, and how to integrate it all into Transformers and vLLM. We will also look at approaches where the second model is not needed at all: EAGLE, Medusa, LayerSkip, and DFlash. Read more

item.title: Why You Can't Just Upload Fitness Tracker History to an LLM and Ask It to Assess Your Health
item.description:
Researchers tested whether large language models could accurately analyze real-world fitness tracker data. Surprisingly, models performed worse at simple calculations on the numbers themselves than at clinical interpretations of the same data. GPT-4o, for instance, correctly identified trends and anomalies only a quarter of the time but was twice as confident in its health risk assessments based on the same data. This suggests a systemic issue where LLMs struggle with direct data analysis compared to applying general knowledge, a problem highlighted by the WearableQA benchmark across 14 models. This article explores the implications for trusting AI with personal health data.

item.title: Publish tools, not pixels: building a WebMCP store with React and counting the pitfalls
item.description:
Imagine a typical online store. A user opens the catalog, types 'headphones' into search, applies the 'in stock' filter, sets a price up to 10,000 rubles, opens the product card, and adds the item to the cart. Six perfectly understandable actions. If a human performs them, everything is fine. If an AI agent takes over, a small quest begins: read the page, find the field, guess the purpose of the toggle, click the button, check the result, and don't accidentally buy a coffee maker instead of headphones. What if the site itself told the agent: 'I can search for products, show product cards, and add items to the cart. Here are the function names, here are the parameters, here are the limitations'? This is the task solved by WebMCP — an experimental browser API that allows a page to declare tools for AI agents directly from JavaScript or an HTML form. The draft and discussion of the standard are open in the Web Machine Learning Community Group repository. My name is Denis Smirnov, I am a lead .NET developer with over five years of experience. This is not a news retelling. I will build a small electronics store using React, add three tools, run checks, and show four pitfalls I encountered. The pitfalls turned out to be more interesting than the working example. Read on

item.title: How we trained a jailbreak detector for Russian-speaking AI agents
item.description:
Hello Habr! The R&D team at Just AI is here. We research NLP and GenAI to ensure the company's products maintain SOTA status in the market. Specifically, we are responsible for guard models and benchmarks for the Jay Guard product, which this article will discuss. Over the past two years, researchers and hackers have discovered numerous ways to steal data through AI assistants. In one case, data from Microsoft 365 tenants was accessed; in another, the contents of private Slack channels. This didn't require an exploit in the traditional sense. Techniques used by social engineers for half a century were employed: gain trust, impersonate authority, ask for a small favor. Only now, instead of a human, the model became the victim. At Just AI, we build guardrails for LLM applications and agents. Our main product in this area is Jay Guard. It's an AI-Security layer between the application and the model, performing checks for attacks, content, and personal data. This article will examine Jay Guard's text detectors and the data they are trained on. We'll discuss why off-the-shelf models produced too many false positives on Russian-language traffic, what changed after data refinement, and what limitations remain. Training the model turned out to be just the beginning; the main work involves continuously maintaining quality against evolving attacks and real user traffic. Read more

item.title: AI isn't cutting routine, but costs. That's why a safety net is now the baseline minimum
item.description:
Everyone is discussing whether AI will take IT jobs. I have no doubt we are only at the beginning of this difficult path. And finding a new job was already a quest with a star. Seeing how "automation" decimates entire departments, I created an app that acts as a navigator to a safety net and goals. It provides peace of mind through a money management system and autopilot, rather than another calculator and analytics of where money went. Read more

item.title: Why the Same Model Can Cost Five Times More
item.description:
Researchers from UC Berkeley and Arena compared seven models within Claude Code, Codex CLI, and the minimalist Pi. On two benchmarks, the choice of harness barely changed the average success rate but increased the cost of the same model by up to five times. The result explains why comparing coding agents by model name alone is already meaningless. Read more

item.title: Artificial intelligence should be owned by natural intelligence: who is responsible for AI errors
item.description:
AI has already taken over ticket routing, standard responses, and half of the first-line work. Where a person used to manually sort out who to send a request about a broken printer to and who to send a request about CRM access to, an algorithm now handles it, one that doesn't get tired by Friday evening and doesn't confuse priorities. A logical question arises: if AI has taken over routine tasks, why is ITSM still needed? The Service Desk's area of responsibility is being redistributed. Let's discuss who is responsible for AI services and what happens if they are left to run on their own. Read more

item.title: Interactive NPC in Unreal Engine. Part 2: RAG, Emotions, and Function Calling
item.description:
In the first part, we built an interactive NPC prototype based on MetaHuman in Unreal Engine. The NPC "heard" the player (STT), processed the recognized text using an LLM (local model inference via llama.cpp), and voiced the response (TTS + lipsync). However, a "talking head" is not yet a character. Such an NPC's understanding of the world is static (hardcoded in the system prompt), it responds emotionlessly and politely to any query, and doesn't affect what's happening in the game. These are precisely the problems we tried to solve. Spoiler: we succeeded. Read more
